units: the takes recorded in the room come out muddy
the technician blames the hard surfaces of the walls
a note played takes too long to die away in the room
the player reports a hum tied to the ventilation system
the first fix is to hang absorbent material near the microphones
the second fix is to set the air duct on flexible mounts
the player fears the tone colour of her instrument will suffer
the technician promises the opposite, a gain in the high frequencies
text: The studio technician kept saying that the takes made in that room came back muddy, and he laid the blame squarely on the bare walls. A note, once played, hung on far too long; by the time it had faded, the next attack was already smeared into it. The cellist added that she could hear a low hum whenever the ventilation started up. Two fixes were put forward. The first was to hang absorbent panels close to the microphones, so that the hard surfaces stopped throwing sound back into the takes. The second was to set the air duct on flexible mounts, which would keep its shudder out of the floor. She worried about what all that might do to the colour of her instrument. The technician promised the opposite: strip out the stray echo, he said, and the top of the sound comes back, the very frequencies the room had been swallowing.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: two ways of handing music on have lived side by side over long stretches of time
the first rests on a pupil copying a master by ear
in that way nothing is set down on any material support
every performer freely alters the piece he has learnt
the second uses written signs giving the pitch and the length
writing pins the work down and lets it travel far from its maker
handing music on by ear breeds many versions
specialists find that the two routes have combined
copyists set down only an outline that performers filled out
text: Two ways of handing music on have lived side by side over long stretches of time, and the contrast between them still shapes how players work. The older one rests on the ear alone: a master plays, a pupil copies, and the piece travels through patient repetition. Nothing is set down on any material support, so every performer bends the tune a little, adds an ornament here, shortens a repeat there. The other relies on written signs that state the pitch and the length of each note. Writing pins the work down and lets it travel far from the person who made it, whereas the route through the ear breeds version upon version. Scholars are clear that the two paths never shut each other out: copyists set down no more than an outline, and it fell to the performers to fill in what the page left silent.

units: every sound comes from a quick movement that stirs the surrounding air
the first family gathers strings stretched between two fixed points
such strings are set going by plucking, bowing or striking them
a hollow box swells the movement passed on by the string
the second family gathers hollow tubes driven by the breath of the player
the pitch got from a tube depends on how much air is left free
the third family covers skins pulled tight over a frame
the fourth family covers metal bars and plates that are struck
each family is known by its colour of sound, tied to the material used
text: Every sound begins with a quick movement that stirs the air around it, and the objects able to make such a movement fall into families. The first gathers strings stretched between two fixed points: pluck them, bow them or strike them, and the shudder they give off passes into a hollow box that swells it. The second brings together hollow tubes, where the breath of the player sets a column of air going, and the pitch depends on how much of that air is left free. The third covers skins pulled tight over a frame, which answer a blow with a short, dark ring. The fourth takes in metal bars and plates that sound of their own accord once they are knocked. Each family carries a colour of its own, because the material set moving filters the overtones of the sound in its own way.

units: a neighbour takes the narrator down to the basement of their building one evening
the neighbour claims the pipes down there give out a kind of singing
the two women go down with a torch and a recorder
at first they hear only the boiler and the metal door
when the pump stops a held low note comes out
a faint high sound goes with that low note
the neighbour admits she has been hearing it for several weeks
playing the take back reveals a steady throb
a tradesman later puts it down to a valve left half shut
text: My neighbour from the flat below dragged me down to the basement one evening, swearing that the pipes down there could sing. We went with a torch and a borrowed recorder. At first, nothing: the boiler grumbling away, the metal door creaking shut behind us. Then the pump stopped, and the whole place began to ring. A low note came up out of the pipework, steady and held, with a thin whistle sitting above it. She was laughing; she said she had been hearing it for weeks and had never dared mention it to anyone. We left the machine running for half an hour. Back upstairs we played the take through, and there it was, clear, with a steady throb running under it. The plumber who came the week after sorted it out in a sentence: a valve left half shut, and a pipe whistling away like a flute.

units: capturing the sounds of a street calls for a strict method
a spot sheltered from moving air has to be chosen
air hitting the diaphragm of the microphone sets off a rumble that buries everything
the machine has to be clamped to a steady stand
a hand holding the microphone passes on audible rubbing
the phone should be switched off to keep out interference
a take should begin before the event aimed at and run on past it
the take should be listened to on headphones before leaving the place
text: Recording the sounds of a street takes far more care than people expect, and every slip shows up later at the editing stage. Pick a sheltered spot first, because moving air hits the diaphragm of the microphone and sets off a rumble that buries everything else. Clamp the machine to a stand next, since a hand holding a microphone passes on the least rub, and you end up with a rasp running the whole length of the take. Switch your phone off: held close, it can throw a short click into the recording that no amount of work will lift out afterwards. Start rolling before the event you are after and let it run on past, or the cut lands too early and the passage is no use to anyone. Listen back on headphones before you leave, because a fault caught late means going again, while one caught early takes a step sideways.

units: a railway line runs right along the playground of a school
passing trains swallow the voices of the children
teachers describe lessons broken off again and again
protective works were carried out over a season
a thick tilted wall throws the sound wave back towards the track
the windows of the building were fitted with heavier glazing
absorbent cladding was hung on the exposed frontage
the noise remains but seems clearly further off
the children can now hear the bell without straining
text: From the school playground, it is not the children you hear first but the railway running along the wall. At regular intervals a train goes by, and the squeal of wheels on the curved rail swallows the voices, the games, even the bell itself. Teachers describe lessons cut to ribbons, dictation started over and over, pupils raising their voices without noticing they are doing it. The building work lasted a season. A thick wall, tilted towards the track, now throws the wave back down onto the ballast instead of letting it clear the fence. The windows were fitted with heavier glazing, and absorbent cladding was hung across the exposed frontage. The rumble has not gone; it has moved off, as though pushed behind a curtain. Out in the yard the bell rises above the voices again, and nobody shouts to be answered.

units: two halls in the same music school sound different
the lower hall is lined with timber set on a hollow frame
its walls take the top off the sound and soften the attack
the upper hall is built of polished stone and has no hangings
its walls send the sound wave back almost untouched
quick notes there pile onto one another
a brass section gains weight in the upper hall
a string quartet loses its clarity there
teachers keep the lower hall for sessions where detail is worked out
text: The lower hall and the upper hall of the music school do not sound alike at all, and the ear picks the difference up within a bar or two. The lower one is lined with timber panels set on a hollow frame. Its walls give a little as the instrument sounds; they take the top off the note and hand back something warm and slightly veiled, in which the bite of the strings is rounded away. The upper hall is built of polished stone, with no hangings and no rugs of any kind. Its walls send the wave back almost untouched, so that quick notes pile onto one another before they have died. A brass section gains weight and body up there, while a string quartet loses its edge and its outline. Teachers therefore keep the lower hall for the sessions where detail has to be worked out, note by note and bar by bar.

units: the writer disputes the idea that music played without a break is harmless
he puts forward three objections in turn
the first objection bears on the draw made on the attention of the customer
that draw brings on a tiredness whose cause escapes the one who feels it
the second objection bears on staff exposed to the same loop of sound
those staff have no control at all over what they hear
the third objection bears on the loss of standing of music itself
the writer holds that silence is what makes a sound audible
text: It would be a mistake to treat the music that plays without a break in shops as a harmless courtesy. Three objections deserve to be set out. The first bears on attention: an unbroken stream of sound draws off part of the mental resources of whoever is buying, who listens without listening and tires without ever placing the cause of that tiredness. The second concerns the staff on the floor, for the person selling, serving or taking payment sits through the same loop from the start of a shift to the end of it, with no control whatever over what reaches their ears. The third bears on music itself, which loses its standing as an event once it becomes a hanging draped behind every activity. Silence is not a gap waiting to be filled; it is the condition that makes a sound audible at all.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the tuner of the theatre began his training very young
he sorted felts in the workshop of an instrument maker
he was first taught to hear the beats between neighbouring strings
he then spent a year replacing hammers
he also adjusted the travel of every key on the keyboard
once a tuner, he went from one concert hall to another
the heat of the lamps threatens the steadiness of the instrument
he says one false note is enough to shake the confidence of an orchestra
he now hands his trade on to two apprentices
text: The tuner at the theatre started learning the trade very young, in the workshop of an instrument maker who set him to sorting felts. He was taught to hear the beats between two neighbouring strings long before anyone put a key in his hand. A whole year then went on replacing hammers and adjusting the travel of every key across the keyboard, painstaking work that asks for a steady hand. Once he was tuning on his own, he went from one concert hall to the next, where the instrument had to hold despite the heat of the lamps and the air stirred up by a crowd. He says that one false note heard from the desk is enough to shake the confidence of a whole orchestra. He now hands the trade on to two apprentices, telling them that the ear is built by patience, and that the hand follows of itself.

units: the concert discussed took place in an old market hall
the metal roof and the concrete floor throw the sound back hard
that layout gives a metallic ring to the returning sound
the trio played more quietly to suit the place
the gaps left between the musical phrases became noticeable
the double bass suffered from too much low end in the space
the drums on the other hand gained from the acoustics
the reviewer advises standing near the stage
text: Honestly, that concert in the old market hall was worth the trip, and what struck me had as much to do with the building as with the players. The roof is sheet metal and the floor bare concrete, so the least note comes straight back at you with a metallic ring, and a loud band would turn to mush in there within a minute of starting. The trio had clearly worked that out: they played quietly, very quietly, and because of it the gaps between the phrases came to count for as much as the notes did. The double bass suffered, since low frequencies gather in a space like that one and end up as a thick paste. The drums, on the other hand, came off well, as every stroke went up into the roof beams and came back broader. One tip if you go: stand right down at the front, close to the stage.
